subtitle: SNMP management of Frame Relay virtual circuits and service parameters.

tldr.problem: Frame Relay providers and their customers need a standard way to monitor the health and performance of Frame Relay virtual circuits, manage service parameters like bandwidth commitments, and receive alerts about failures.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines SNMP MIB objects for Frame Relay service, including logical port configuration, virtual circuit signaling parameters, per-VC statistics, and accounting objects. The MIB is designed for Customer Network Management, allowing customers to see their own PVCs and service endpoints via SNMP.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides the standardized vocabulary for Frame Relay network management. It was corrected and superseded by RFC 2954. Frame Relay itself has largely faded as Ethernet and IP became dominant, but the management architecture live on in other virtual circuit technologies.

today: RFC 1604 was obsoleted by RFC 2954. Frame Relay was popular in the 1990s as a wide-area network service connecting corporate offices, but has largely been replaced by MPLS VPNs, Ethernet services, and the internet itself. The concept of virtual circuits and service parameters like CIR lives on in MPLS, which uses similar concepts to offer service guarantees.

sections.title: Frame Relay Service Management
sections.content:
Frame Relay is a network service that lets organizations share a "cloud" of connectivity from a carrier. Instead of buying a dedicated line between each pair of offices, a company buys Frame Relay service and the carrier creates virtual circuits connecting the customer's sites through a shared network. The carrier multiplexes traffic from many customers on the same physical links.

Unlike older technologies like X.25, Frame Relay assumes the underlying physical layer is relatively reliable, so it does not do extensive error checking. Instead, it focuses on switching packets (called "frames") between the customer's sites, identified by DLCI (Data Link Connection Identifier) numbers.

This RFC defines SNMP management objects for the Frame Relay service provider to expose to customers via a proxy agent. The customer can poll these objects to monitor their virtual circuits, learn about failures, and confirm their service parameters.
sections.eli5: Your office has a shared connection to the phone company's network. Frames with a special label say which office they are going to. This document lists what the phone company will tell you about your frames and circuits if you ask via network management.

sections.title: Frame Relay Concepts and Architecture
sections.content:
UNI (User-to-Network Interface) is the connection between a customer's equipment and the Frame Relay network. NNI (Network-to-Network Interface) is the connection between two Frame Relay networks. A DLCI (Data Link Connection Identifier) is a label (10 to 23 bits depending on the format) that identifies a particular PVC (Permanent Virtual Connection) at a given UNI or NNI port.

A PVC is a pre-established virtual circuit. The customer's router or switch sends frames with the PVC's DLCI across its UNI, and the Frame Relay network delivers them to the other end of the PVC. This is simpler than connection setup on each transmission.

The service is characterized by CIR (Committed Information Rate)—the rate at which the network commits to deliver frames. Bc (Committed Burst Size) is the maximum amount of data the network will transfer in a time interval Tc. Be (Excess Burst Size) is additional data the network will attempt to deliver, but with lower priority.

The RFC covers what a service provider's proxy agent exposes about Frame Relay service: logical ports, VC signaling parameters, per-VC statistics, and accounting information. The management model is based on Customer Network Management (CNM), where the customer's NMS (Network Management Station) queries the carrier's proxy agent to see only its own PVCs and ports.
sections.eli5: The network has labeled boxes (PVCs) that carry your frames. Each box has a number label (DLCI). The network promises to move a certain amount per second (CIR). You can send faster, but the extra is not guaranteed. You ask the phone company's network manager (via SNMP) what is happening to your boxes.

sections.title: MIB Objects and Tables
sections.content:
The RFC defines five main groups of managed objects:

Logical Port Group: One entry per Frame Relay UNI or NNI logical port. For each port, it records the address numbering plan (E.164, X.121, or none), contact information, location, whether it is a UNI or NNI, the Q.922 address field length and DLCI length, and the virtual circuit signaling protocol in use (LMI, ANSI T1.617D, ANSI T1.617B, CCITT Q.933A, or none).

Management VC Signaling Group: Per-port signaling parameters and errors. This includes user-side and network-side timers and thresholds (N391, N392, N393, T391, T392, nN4, nT3) for link integrity verification and error detection. It also tracks signaling errors such as link reliability errors, protocol errors, and channel inactivity.

PVC End-Point Group: Per-VC statistics at the end-point. Each PVC has a DLCI and an ifIndex (the port it belongs to). Statistics include transmitted and received octets and frames, discarded and errored frames, and the CIR, Bc, and Be parameters.

Frame Relay PVC Connection Group: Connection status and type information, including whether the PVC is active or deleted and the local and remote DLCI values for two-point circuits.

Accounting Groups: Usage statistics for billing, such as octets transmitted and received per VC per accounting interval.
sections.eli5: The MIB has tables for ports, for the signaling procedures, for each virtual circuit's statistics, for connection status, and for billing counts. You can query them to see what is happening to each circuit and what the phone company is measuring.

sections.title: Customer Network Management and Proxy Agents
sections.content:
The MIB is designed for Customer Network Management. The Frame Relay network provider operates a proxy agent—an SNMP agent that represents the carrier's Frame Relay equipment. The customer's Network Management Station connects to the proxy agent, typically via SNMP over IP encapsulated in a Frame Relay PVC (according to RFC 1490).

The proxy agent exposes only the customer's own ports and PVCs; it enforces instance-level granularity so that a customer cannot see another customer's circuits. The customer can retrieve operational status, performance statistics, and configuration parameters, and can typically receive SNMP traps when events like PVC state changes or error thresholds are exceeded.

If a customer's PVCs traverse multiple Frame Relay networks, the customer must query multiple proxy agents (one per network) to get an end-to-end view of service.
sections.eli5: The phone company runs a special agent that talks SNMP. You connect to it via SNMP to ask about your circuits. It only shows you your own circuits, not anyone else's. If you go through multiple phone companies, you have to ask each one.

sections.title: SNMPv2 and MIB-II Integration
sections.content:
This RFC uses SNMPv2 (as opposed to the original SNMPv1). Frame Relay logical ports are represented as entries in the standard ifTable from MIB-II, with an ifType value of 44. Standard ifTable objects like ifSpeed, ifAdminStatus, ifOperStatus, ifInOctets, ifOutOctets, ifInErrors, and ifOutErrors apply, along with Frame Relay–specific extensions.

For example, ifSpeed is set to the user data rate of the Frame Relay port (the committed or peak bandwidth available). Frame Relay ports support the ifStackTable (Interfaces Stack Group) for representing the relationship between logical ports and their underlying physical interfaces.

The RFC also defines Frame Relay–specific traps (notifications) that the proxy agent can send to alert the customer about events such as changes in PVC status, signaling errors, or violations of accounting rules.
sections.eli5: The Frame Relay data fits into the standard SNMP MIB structure. The port looks like a regular network interface in the ifTable. Your network management tool can query it the same way it queries Ethernet ports, but gets Frame Relay-specific information too.

viz.caption: Key Frame Relay service parameters and what they control

items.title: DLCI
items.text: Data Link Connection Identifier—the virtual circuit's unique label at a UNI or NNI port.

items.title: CIR
items.text: Committed Information Rate—the minimum speed the network promises for this PVC.

items.title: Bc
items.text: Committed Burst Size—the maximum data burst the network commits to deliver in time interval Tc.

items.title: Be
items.text: Excess Burst Size—additional data the network will try to deliver, but with lower priority.

items.title: UNI / NNI
items.text: User-to-Network Interface or Network-to-Network Interface: the type of port.

items.title: PVC
items.text: Permanent Virtual Connection: a pre-established virtual circuit across the Frame Relay network.
